html:
The Sanxingdui bronzes are a hoard of strange and striking bronze objects found at Sanxingdui, near Chengdu in Sichuan, southwest China. They date to around the 12th and 11th centuries BCE.

Local farmers found jade objects there in the late 1920s, but the great find came in 1986, when archaeologists opened two pits full of buried treasure. More pits were opened from 2020. They held:

  • Bronze heads and masks with huge eyes, some with pupils sticking far out of the face, and large ears.
  • A bronze figure of a man about 2.6 metres tall, standing on a pedestal.
  • Bronze trees with birds on their branches.
  • Gold masks and a gold covered staff, plus many elephant tusks.

They are contemporary with the late Shang dynasty in the Yellow River valley but look nothing like Shang art. They show that China in the Bronze Age had more than one centre of civilisation. No writing was found, so the people's own name is unknown; many link them to the ancient kingdom of Shu. The later Jinsha site in Chengdu seems to carry on their culture.
